You choose the right congiuntivo tense according to the tense of the main verb: spero che venga / sia venuto, but speravo che venisse / fosse venuto / sarebbe venuto; vorrei che tu fossi qui.
I hoped you would notice me.
I thought you had never seen me.
I hope that one day you'll read these letters.
I thought he would come back the next day.
To choose the congiuntivo after a main verb in the present: penso che sia (now), che sia stato (before), che sarà (after).
To choose the congiuntivo after a main verb in the past: pensavo che fosse, che fosse stato, che sarebbe stato.
To use the past conditional for the future in the past: speravo che sarebbe venuto.
To use vorrei che + congiuntivo imperfetto for wishes.
To recognise the same logic with the indicative: so che è / sapevo che era.
To read and write a personal letter with feelings and memories.

Florence, July. The workers repairing the building's roof have found a tin box in the attic with twelve unopened letters addressed to Graziella. The handwriting is Aldo's. Graziella reads one of them with Giulia and Pietro.
They're from 1974 and '75. He wrote one a month. But he never sent them.
"Dear Graziella, today I ate ribollita for the thirtieth time. I hoped you would notice me, but I think you haven't even seen me."
Grandma, why does Grandpa write "speravo che tu mi notassi" and not "speravo che tu mi notavi"?
Because after "sperare" you need the congiuntivo. And since "speravo" is in the past, the congiuntivo goes into the imperfetto: notassi.
And "credo che tu non mi abbia visto"?
"Credo" is in the present, and the seeing happened before. So congiuntivo passato: abbia visto.
You've already started on grammar? I'm crying and you're giving a lesson!
Sorry, Grandma. Will you read some more?
"I wish you knew who I am. But I fear your father has already taken me for a tramp."
And had your father taken him for a tramp?
Yes. My dad thought he was a penniless student who would disappear after a week. Instead he stayed fifty years.
that you would notice me (cong. imperfetto)
Double SS: FOS-si, FOS-se. Don't confuse with "fosti" (passato remoto).
1. Main verb in the present or future
Credo che tu non mi abbia visto.
The key question: does the action in the subordinate clause happen at the same time as, before or after the main verb?
2. Main verb in the past or conditional
Credevo che non mi avessi mai visto.
Pensavo che sarebbe sparito dopo una settimana.
The most common mistake: "Pensavo che tu sia stanco". If the main verb is in the past, the correct form is "Pensavo che tu fossi stanco".
Learn these three rows by heart with a single verb (venire). Then swap in any other verb.
After verbs in the conditional (vorrei, preferirei, mi piacerebbe), the congiuntivo is in the imperfetto, even if the wish is for now:
Vorrei che il nonno fosse qui.
Mi piacerebbe che leggessi queste lettere.
I'd like you to read these letters.
Avrei voluto che tu lo sapessi.
NOT: "Vorrei che tu sia qui." Correct: "Vorrei che tu fossi qui."
5. The same logic with the indicative
The sequence of tenses is a system: the main verb "pulls" the tenses of the subordinate clause along with it. You saw the same mechanism in chapter 61, with reported speech.
I think you haven't seen me.
I thought he would disappear after a week.
I feared your father didn't want me.
I knew he would come back.
Dove sono state trovate le lettere?

Perché Graziella si arrabbia un po’?

The work on the roof of the Via Maggio building had started in mid-July, as provided for in the agreement with Arno Living. For three weeks the trattoria had lived under scaffolding, with the noise of hammers instead of the radio and dust coming in through the windows despite the plastic sheets. The builders had lunch in the trattoria every day, and Graziella, who at first eyed them with suspicion, had ended up adopting them: she had even taught the site foreman, a Calabrian called Rocco, to make ribollita properly.

It was Rocco himself who, one Tuesday morning, came down from the attic with a tin box in his hand. It was an old biscuit tin, rusty at the corners, with the faded picture of a lady with a parasol. "Signora Graziella," he said, taking off his helmet, "we found it under the roof tiles, in a hole in the wall, near the big beam. Your name is written on it." And indeed, on the lid, in a marker pen that time had almost erased, was written: "For Graziella. When I have the courage".

Graziella recognised the handwriting before she even read the words. She sat down, very slowly, on the nearest chair. Nobody dared speak. Rocco stood with his helmet in his hand, as if in church. Inside the box were twelve envelopes tied with string, all sealed, all with the stamp already stuck on and no postmark. On each was the trattoria's address and a date: March 1974, April 1974, May 1974… up to February 1975. Aldo had written them, bought the stamps, and never sent them.

"Twelve letters," said Pietro, who knew the story better than anyone because he had written it in his essay. "Twelve months of ribollita before he asked you to the cinema. One letter for each month!" Graziella looked at the first envelope. "He'd counted them," she said softly. "He told me years later: he said he'd eaten three hundred and twenty ribollitas before he found the courage. I thought he was joking." Then she opened the envelope, her hands trembling.

The first letter was short. "Dear Graziella (may I call you that? I heard your father say it), today I came into your trattoria and ordered ribollita. I told you it was the best in Florence, and you answered 'I know'. I thought you would laugh in my face, and instead you smiled. I hoped you would recognise me, but I think you don't remember me. That's all right. I'll be back. Aldo." Graziella read it twice, then passed it to Giulia without a word.

The following letters told, month by month, the same story seen from the other side of the table. In April Aldo wrote that he had found work at a printing shop in San Frediano and could eat at the trattoria every day, "if your father doesn't throw me out". And he added: "Today I ate ribollita for the thirtieth time. I hoped you would notice me, but I think you haven't even seen me. I haven't slept for three nights."

In May the letter was longer and more worried. "Your father looks at me as if I were a thief. Yesterday he asked me what I did for a living, and when I told him I'm a printer, he said: 'Ah. Lead letters.' I didn't understand if it was a compliment. I'm afraid he thinks I'm one of those '68 boys who don't want to work. I wish he knew that I work ten hours a day. Above all, I wish you knew."

Pietro listened open-mouthed. Every so often, when Giulia read a sentence, he repeated it under his breath, as if he wanted to learn it by heart. At one point he took his school exercise book and began copying out some sentences. "What are you doing?" asked Marco, who had come down from his office as soon as he heard about the box. "Grandpa writes better than my grammar book," answered Pietro. "Look: 'Speravo che mi guardassi', 'Temo che pensi', 'Vorrei che sapesse'. He got all the subjunctives right. Without even thinking about it."

"He was a printer," said Marco, with a slightly sad smile. "For years he set newspaper pages letter by letter, backwards, in lead. He used to say that anyone who has set a wrong subjunctive by hand and had to redo the whole line never gets it wrong again for the rest of his life." Marco took the May letter and held it up to the light, as if looking for something between the lines. "I didn't know he'd been so afraid of Grandpa," he said. "He never talked to me about it."

The summer letters were full of little things: the August heat, the trattoria closed for the holidays ("fifteen days without seeing you: I thought they would never end"), a trip to Fiesole where he had seen Graziella from a distance with her friends and hadn't had the courage to say hello. In September he wrote that he had bought two cinema tickets but had let them expire in his pocket. In October, that he had bought them again. In November, that he had let them expire again.

It was the November letter that made everyone laugh, for the first time since the box had been opened. "Dear Graziella, eight years have passed since I first saw you, in the mud, with the loaf in your hand. You don't remember. I do. Today I bought the tickets for the third time. The cashier at the Odeon cinema knows me by now and asked me if I was sure this time. I told him yes. Then I came to the trattoria and ordered ribollita. As always."

Graziella wiped her eyes with her apron. "Eight years," she repeated. "In '66 I was twelve, and he was eighteen. Eight years, and he never told me, my Aldo." "So he really did remember," said Pietro softly. "You always said it: he pretended to forget the beautiful things. But he didn't forget them." Graziella nodded, unable to speak. In the trattoria, at that moment, all you could hear was a builder's hammer on the roof, far away, like a heartbeat.

The last letter, the one from February '75, was different from the others. It was written more calmly, in the tidy handwriting of someone who has made a decision. "Dear Graziella, I have decided not to send you these letters. I'm putting them in this box and hiding it in a place where nobody will find it for a long time. Tomorrow I'll ask you to the cinema. Out loud, looking you in the eyes, as it should be done. If you say yes, I hope that one day you'll read these letters and laugh at me. If you say no, I'd rather you never read them."

There was a long silence. Then Giulia, who was folding the letter back up, noticed something. "But how did he manage to hide it here, in the attic, in February '75? He didn't live in this building yet." Graziella smiled at last, her eyes still wet. "No," she said. "But my dad did. And in February my dad had called a young man to fix the roof, because it was raining into the kitchen. A tall, thin young man who worked for free."

"Grandpa?" asked Pietro. "Grandpa," confirmed Graziella. "My dad thought he was a tramp, but a tramp who fixed roofs for free suited him fine. That's how he started to trust him. And the day after he finished the roof, Aldo asked me to the cinema. I don't remember the film. I remember he held the tickets in his hand the whole time, as if he was afraid they'd expire again." Rocco, the foreman, blew his nose noisily. "Sorry," he said. "It's the dust." Then he went back up to the roof without another word, and all afternoon the builders worked in an unusual, almost respectful silence, as if there were still something under the tiles to protect.

That evening Graziella did something nobody expected. She took a sheet of paper, an envelope and a stamp, and sat down at the table by the window. She wrote for an hour, crossing out and starting again, as she had done for the Palazzo Vecchio speech. Then she sealed the envelope, wrote on it "For Aldo. Now that I've found the courage", and put it in the tin box with the other twelve. Nobody asked her what she had written. But the next morning Pietro found a forgotten rough draft on the table, and couldn't resist.

There were only a few lines, full of crossings-out. "Dear Aldo, I thought you were just a shy boy with a red bicycle. I didn't know you had already seen me in the mud, or that you had written twelve letters. If I'd known, I'd have said yes back in March, and we'd have gained a year. I wish you were here to laugh at me, as you wanted. I hope that from up there you've seen the new roof. A Calabrian redid it, but almost as well as you. The ribollita is still the best in Florence. I know."

Pietro put the draft back exactly where it had been, without telling anyone. But that day at lunch, when Rocco and the builders sat down at their usual table, Pietro brought them the ribollita himself and said to Rocco, very seriously: "Thank you for finding the box. If you hadn't found it, Grandma would never have known how shy Grandpa was." Rocco looked at him, then at Graziella behind the counter, who was pretending not to listen. "Young man," he replied, "in thirty years of building sites I've found all sorts of things under roofs. But something like this, never. I'd rather my wife didn't find out, or she'll ask me why I've never written her so much as a postcard."

The tin box, with its thirteen envelopes, did not go back to the attic. Graziella put it on the kitchen shelf, next to the photo of Aldo with the red bicycle and the brush with the blue bristles. Sometimes, in the evening, when the trattoria was closed, Pietro saw her open an envelope at random and reread it, glasses on the tip of her nose, smiling. One evening he asked her which was her favourite. Graziella didn't hesitate. "The March one," she said. "The one where he writes that he thought I'd laugh in his face. Poor Aldo. He hadn't understood that I was laughing because it was the first time anyone had paid me a compliment on my ribollita. And that I'd been hoping for months that he'd come back."
